SHORT VERSION: Do not treat this as 'too old, so I can ignore it.' Whether the debt is time-barred is genuinely arguable on your dates, and limitations in Texas is a defense you LOSE if you don't plead it (Tex. R. Civ. P. 94). Your 14-day answer window ran out two days ago, so the single most urgent thing is to find out whether a default judgment has already been signed and to file an answer TODAY if it has not.

1) IS IT TOO OLD? Texas gives four years to sue on a debt (Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code § 16.004(a)(3)), measured from accrual to the date the plaintiff FILED suit -- not to today. Your petition is file-stamped July 14, 2025. On a revolving account like a store card, accrual is generally the date of default/acceleration (the charge-off and demand for the full balance), but Texas case law is not settled and some courts fix it at the first missed payment. Running both:
  - Charge-off / demand for full balance: November 2021 + 4 years = November 2025. Suit filed July 14, 2025 is INSIDE that -- timely.
  - First missed payment: April 2021 + 4 years = April 2025. Suit filed July 14, 2025 is roughly 3 months AFTER that -- barred.
  - Last payment, March 2021, is NOT the accrual date under the corrected rule, so ignore the March 2025 date you may have computed.
So the limitations defense is a real, live argument, but it is not automatic. It is exactly the kind of accrual question a licensed Texas consumer-debt attorney should evaluate -- plead it, don't assume it.
  TWO EXTRA POINTS FOR YOUR LAWYER: (a) The suit was filed July 14, 2025 but you were not served until September 1, 2026 -- about 13.5 months later. Under Texas law, filing only stops the clock if the plaintiff then used diligence in getting you served; a delay that long is worth raising. (b) If your card agreement has a choice-of-law clause (Delaware, Utah, South Dakota), some of those states have a 3-year period. Texas usually applies its own 4 years, but the clause is worth flagging.

2) DO YOU HAVE TO RESPOND? YES. A time-barred debt still produces a default judgment against a defendant who never answers. This is a debt-claim case in a Harris County justice court (not an eviction), so the answer was due 14 days after service: served Tuesday, September 1, 2026 + 14 days = Tuesday, September 15, 2026 (a business day, so no extension). Today is September 17, 2026, so the deadline was 2 days ago.

3) WHAT TO DO RIGHT NOW -- this depends on one fact I don't have: whether the court has already SIGNED a default judgment.
  - IF NO DEFAULT JUDGMENT HAS BEEN SIGNED: a late answer is still effective. A default judgment cannot be entered while an answer is on file. File a written answer with that justice court TODAY -- filing an answer is free -- and expressly plead the statute of limitations as an affirmative defense (TRCP 94). Call the JP court clerk this morning and ask (a) whether a default judgment has been signed and (b) the case number/how to file.
  - IF A DEFAULT JUDGMENT HAS ALREADY BEEN SIGNED: two short, hard deadlines run from the date the judge SIGNED it: a motion to set aside / new trial within 14 days (TRCP 505.3), and an appeal to county court for a brand-new trial within 21 days of the signing (or of denial of that motion) (TRCP 506.1(a)), perfected by a bond, cash deposit, or a sworn statement of inability to pay. The 21-day appeal requires no excuse for the default. Get the signing date from the clerk and count from it. After 21 days, the remaining routes are equitable and you need a lawyer immediately.

4) VENUE: You are entitled to be sued in the county AND the justice precinct where you live (TRCP 502.4(b)). Harris County has many precincts. If this was filed in the wrong precinct, a sworn motion to transfer venue is due no later than 21 days after your answer is filed (502.4(d)); filing your answer first does not waive it.

5) One more thing to check and tell your lawyer: whether you made ANY payment after the default (a small 'good faith' payment). Under § 16.065 only a signed written acknowledgment can revive a barred claim, and because the plaintiff here is a debt buyer, Tex. Fin. Code § 392.307(c)-(d) says a payment or reaffirmation does NOT revive a time-barred consumer debt and bars the debt buyer from suing on it at all. Also flag anything that might toll the clock (time living outside Texas, military service, unsound mind) -- tolling is a separate analysis not resolved here.

Short version: your deadline has NOT passed, and under every possible scenario you have at least until Tuesday, September 29, 2026 — but I can't give you the exact date without one more fact.

Why. What happened to you is 'substituted service' under Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 415.20: the process server left the summons and complaint at your home with an adult who lives there (your son) instead of handing them to you. For substituted service, the law does not start your clock on the day the papers were dropped off. The statute says the server must ALSO mail a copy of the summons and complaint to you by first-class mail at that address, and '[s]ervice of a summons in this manner is deemed complete on the 10th day after the mailing.' Your 30 days to respond (CCP § 412.20(a)(3)) runs from that deemed-complete date, not from August 20.

The arithmetic:
• Best case for the plaintiff (mailing on the same day, August 20, 2026): service deemed complete August 20 + 10 days = August 30, 2026. Answer due August 30 + 30 days = TUESDAY, SEPTEMBER 29, 2026.
• If the follow-up mailing went out later than August 20 — which is common — every day of delay pushes your deadline one day later. Example: mailed August 27 → complete September 6 → answer due October 6, 2026.
• If no follow-up mailing was ever made, the substituted service is not complete at all and no 30-day clock has started (that would be a service defect — see below).

So as of today, September 17, 2026, you are 12 days or more away from your deadline. Nobody can take a default against you today.

The missing fact and how to get it: the DATE THE PROCESS SERVER MAILED the copy to you. Find it on the Proof of Service (Judicial Council form POS-010) that the server filed with the court — item 5.b lists the date and place of mailing. You can see it by calling the court clerk with the case number, checking the court's online case portal, or looking at the papers your son received. Do that this week. Until you confirm it, plan on September 29, 2026 as your deadline — that is the earliest date it can possibly be, so meeting it is safe under every scenario.

Four things the rule warns about that matter for you:
1) Fee or fee waiver. A limited-civil answer is rejected by the clerk unless it comes with the first-appearance filing fee or a fee-waiver application (form FW-001). A rejected answer does NOT stop a default. File the FW-001 together with your answer if you can't pay. (Source named in the rule node, not quoted — confirm the current fee with the clerk.)
2) Plead your defenses, don't just deny. Under CCP § 431.30(b)(2) any affirmative defense you don't plead is waived. On a credit-card debt-buyer case the big ones are the statute of limitations (plead it by section — CCP § 337 or § 339), lack of standing/no proof of assignment, payment, and identity theft if applicable. Form PLD-050 has an affirmative-defenses section. A timely bare general denial on a stale debt is a timely surrender.
3) Service objections. You say the address is your home and you don't dispute that, so a motion to quash under CCP § 418.10 probably isn't your route — but note that if it turns out no follow-up mailing was ever made, service was never completed, and in that situation filing an answer first would be a general appearance that waives the objection entirely. That is another reason to check the POS-010 before you file anything.
4) Other timely responses. A demurrer or motion to strike filed within the same window is also a timely response and stops the default clock; if overruled, your answer is then due in the time the court sets or 10 days after notice of the ruling (CCP § 472a(b)).

If you ever do slip past the deadline: an answer filed before the clerk actually ENTERS a default still defeats the default request (CCP § 585), and if a default is entered, CCP § 473(b) allows a motion for relief for mistake, inadvertence, surprise or excusable neglect within six months.

Short answer: under the regulation's mailbox-rule computation, your written dispute is timely if it is sent (and ideally received) by **Wednesday, October 14, 2026** — and to be safe you should send it now, well before early October. Here is the arithmetic.

Step 1 — Date the collector provided the validation information: Friday, September 4, 2026 (the first letter, which was itself the validation notice; that satisfies the timing rule in 15 U.S.C. § 1692g(a) / 12 C.F.R. § 1006.34(a)(1)(i)(A)).

Step 2 — Assumed receipt date. Under 12 C.F.R. § 1006.34(b)(5), the collector may assume you received the notice 5 days after it was provided, counting only days that are NOT Saturdays, Sundays, or federal legal holidays. Counting forward from Sept. 4:
- Sat Sept 5 — excluded
- Sun Sept 6 — excluded
- Mon Sept 7 (Labor Day, federal holiday) — excluded
- Tue Sept 8 = day 1
- Wed Sept 9 = day 2
- Thu Sept 10 = day 3
- Fri Sept 11 = day 4
- Sat Sept 12 / Sun Sept 13 — excluded
- Mon Sept 14 = day 5
Assumed receipt = **Monday, September 14, 2026**.

Step 3 — Add the 30-day dispute window. Important: the weekend/holiday exclusion applies ONLY to the 5-day receipt assumption; the 30 days that follow run in ordinary calendar days. September 14 + 30 calendar days = 16 days to September 30, plus 14 more days = **October 14, 2026**. That is almost certainly the end date printed on the page you misplaced, because collectors compute that disclosure from the same assumed-receipt date.

Step 4 — Where you stand today. Today is September 17, 2026, which is before October 14, so the window is open. Nothing here says you are out of time.

One caution that argues for acting immediately rather than waiting: the statute and § 1006.34(b)(5) measure the 30 days from the date you actually receive the notice OR are assumed to receive it. The facts do not say what day the letter actually landed in your mailbox. A letter mailed Friday Sept. 4 with Labor Day intervening could plausibly have arrived Tuesday Sept. 8 or Wednesday Sept. 9; 30 days from Sept. 8 would be October 8. The collector is permitted to use the Sept. 14 assumed date (and that is the date its own notice will have disclosed), so October 14 is the operative deadline under this node — but you eliminate any argument about it by sending the dispute well before October 8. Send it today or this week.

How to send it so it does what you want:
1. Put it IN WRITING. An oral dispute by phone does not trigger the § 1692g(b) cease-collection duty (that duty by its text requires a writing). (If you have already disputed only by phone and they report this account to a credit bureau without marking it disputed, that is a separate potential violation under 15 U.S.C. § 1692e(8).)
2. Mail it to the collector's address for disputes shown on the notice; use certified mail, return receipt requested, and keep a copy and the receipt so you can prove the send date.
3. Consider also including — in the same letter — a written request for the name and address of the ORIGINAL creditor. Under § 1692g(b) that is a second, independent trigger: it obligates the collector to stop collecting until it mails you that name and address, even apart from the dispute.

What happens next: once your timely written dispute arrives, the collector must cease collection of the disputed debt (or disputed portion) until it obtains verification of the debt or a copy of a judgment and mails that verification to you (15 U.S.C. § 1692g(b); 12 C.F.R. § 1006.38). If it keeps collecting before mailing verification, that is a potential § 1692g(b) violation worth documenting.

Two things to watch that could change the analysis, neither of which appears to be a problem on your facts: (a) this rule only applies to a covered 'debt collector' under 15 U.S.C. § 1692a(6) — a third-party agency collecting someone else's defaulted medical bill normally qualifies, but an original creditor collecting its own debt would not; and (b) if any collection communication you receive during this window demands payment in fewer than 30 days or otherwise pressures you in a way that contradicts your dispute rights, that can be a separate 'overshadowing' violation under § 1692g(b)'s final sentence — save any such letters.

Short answer: your deadline depends on the date the process server MAILED a second copy to you — and that date isn't in your facts. Here's how it works and what the earliest possible deadline is.

1) What happened is 'substituted service' (California Code of Civil Procedure § 415.20(b)). For a limited civil collection case, leaving the summons and complaint with a competent household member 18 or older at your dwelling is only HALF of valid substituted service. The server must ALSO mail a copy of the summons and complaint by first-class mail, postage prepaid, to you at the address where the papers were left.

2) When service is legally 'complete': under § 415.20(b), service is deemed complete on the 10th day AFTER that mailing — not on the day the papers were handed to your son.

3) How long you then have: the summons must tell you that you have 30 days after service is complete to file a written response (CCP § 412.20(a)(3)). Under CCP §§ 12 and 12a, you count calendar days, and if the last day falls on a weekend or court holiday it rolls to the next court day.

Date math, earliest-possible scenario (mailing on the same day the papers were left, Thursday Aug. 20, 2026):
- Aug. 20 + 10 days = Aug. 30, 2026 → service complete Aug. 30, 2026.
- Aug. 30 + 30 days = Sept. 29, 2026 (Aug. 31 is day 1; Sept. 29 is day 30). Sept. 29, 2026 is a Tuesday, not a court holiday.
- So the EARLIEST your response could be due is Tuesday, September 29, 2026 — 12 days from today (Sept. 17, 2026).

Other scenarios:
- If the mailing happened a day or more later (e.g., mailed Friday Aug. 21): service complete Aug. 31, response due Sept. 30, 2026. In general: mailing date + 10 days + 30 days, rolled forward to the next court day if it lands on a weekend/holiday.
- If NO mailing was ever made, substituted service was never completed and no response clock has started at all. But do not rely on that without verifying — the plaintiff may have filed a proof of service stating a mailing date, and a default could be sought based on it.

What to do right now (this week):
- Look through your mail for the envelope from the process server or the law firm; note the postmark/date.
- Check the court's file (in person or online) for the filed Proof of Service of Summons (Judicial Council Form POS-010). Item 5.b on that form states the date and place of mailing. That document tells you the exact date your clock started.
- Until you confirm, treat Tuesday, September 29, 2026 as your deadline. Nothing is lost by responding early, and a default cannot properly be entered before the deadline runs.
- Your response can be an Answer (e.g., Judicial Council Form PLD-C-010 for contract/collection cases, with the correct filing fee or a fee waiver request, Form FW-001), or a demurrer/motion. If you want to challenge the service itself as defective (for example, no mailing was ever made), a motion to quash service under CCP § 418.10 must be filed on or before the last day to respond — filing an Answer first waives that objection.
- You can also ask the collector's attorney in writing for a stipulated extension of time to respond; these are commonly granted, but get it in writing and, if possible, filed with the court.

Nothing here says any deadline has passed — as of today, September 17, 2026, you still have time under every version of the facts. Because the exact deadline turns on the mailing date and because a missed deadline can lead to a default judgment, consider contacting a California consumer attorney or your local legal aid/self-help center promptly.

Short answer: the 30 days runs from the day you RECEIVED the letter, not the day it was mailed, so I need your actual receipt date to give you one firm date. Here is the arithmetic and the safe date.

The rule: Under the FDCPA, 15 U.S.C. § 1692g(b), if you notify the collector IN WRITING within 30 days after you receive the validation notice that you dispute the debt (or any part of it), the collector must cease collection of the debt until it mails you verification. Under Regulation F, 12 C.F.R. § 1006.34(b)(5), the 'validation period' ends 30 days after you receive the notice, and the collector is allowed to presume you received it on the fifth day after mailing, counting every day except Sundays and federal legal public holidays.

Applying the presumption to your facts (mailed Friday, Sept. 4, 2026):
• Sat. Sept. 5 = day 1
• Sun. Sept. 6 = not counted (Sunday)
• Mon. Sept. 7 = not counted (Labor Day, federal holiday)
• Tue. Sept. 8 = day 2
• Wed. Sept. 9 = day 3
• Thu. Sept. 10 = day 4
• Fri. Sept. 11 = day 5 → presumed receipt date
Then 30 days after Sept. 11: Sept. 11 + 19 days = Sept. 30; + 11 more days = Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026. Because Oct. 11 is a Sunday and the FDCPA has no express weekend roll-over rule for this period, the practical outside date under the presumption is Friday, Oct. 9, 2026.

Alternatives depending on when you actually received it (the statute measures from actual receipt):
• Received Sat. Sept. 5, 2026 → 30 days ends Monday, Oct. 5, 2026.
• Received Tue. Sept. 8, 2026 → 30 days ends Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026.
• Received Fri. Sept. 11, 2026 (the presumed date) → 30 days ends Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026; send by Fri., Oct. 9, 2026.

Safest course: mail your written dispute so it is postmarked no later than Friday, October 2, 2026. That is within 30 days even under the earliest possible receipt date (Sept. 5), so no one can argue you were late. Send it certified mail, return receipt requested (or keep proof of mailing plus a copy), say clearly 'I dispute this debt' and, if you want the original creditor's name and address, add 'I request the name and address of the original creditor.' You can also use any dispute link/QR code or phone option the notice lists, but put it in writing too — the cease-collection right in § 1692g(b) is triggered by a written dispute.

Two more things: (1) You do not need the missing page to dispute; there is no required form or wording. (2) If you miss the 30-day window, you can still dispute — the collector simply is not required to stop collecting while it verifies, and it must still not misrepresent the debt or report it to a credit bureau without noting the dispute (15 U.S.C. §§ 1692e(8), 1692g(b)). You can also ask the collector to re-send the validation notice or send you the missing page.
